questions.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $F$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $F,$ then $F$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $F=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $F,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
F={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -10 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-26 & -30 \\ 24 & 28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $L$ given that 

$$
L[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $L:$

$$
L={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $L$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $L$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$
$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$

questions.problem:
Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $T$ given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]T=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the matrix $[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -7\end{aligned}]$

B={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $B$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $\mathcal{B}= \{ \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $C,$ then $C$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $C=PDP^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $C,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order: 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069457/assets/1cf1ba5d93618341227836a110479ebfc258894f9d4f60ae4df1be682d7c74fc.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain
